pages.text: "Six, seven..." Riri folded her fingers one by one under the covers. She would get up at ten. But after ten, she said, "Back to one!" and counted again.
Lolo put on boots and bounced by the door. "Riri, Dad's boat is leaving!" "I want to wave goodbye too! Just ten more!" Riri pulled the covers to her chin.
Putt, putt, putt—the sound grew quieter in the distance. Dropping the covers, Riri leaned on the windowsill. "Dad! I am here!" Though she called, the boat grew smaller.
That evening, Dad returned. Riri's shoulders drooped. He sat beside her. "Riri, my boat goes putt, putt, putt before it leaves. That is your signal."
"When you hear it, do this instead of counting." Dad pretended to fling back covers and plant both feet on the floor. Riri planted her feet, copying him.
Lolo pointed beneath the bed. "My boots are here, so I can put them on quickly." Riri put her yellow hat by her bed too. Dad smiled and sang, "Hear putt, putt, putt—jump up!"
At dawn the next day, putt, putt, putt! Riri threw back the covers and planted both feet on the floor. She did not count. She reached out and pulled on her hat.
Dad's boat was still moored at the pier. Riri stood by the rope. Dad paused while untying it and looked at her. "Our Riri is here to see me off today!"
Riri ran to the end of the pier. "One, hear putt, putt, putt—jump up! Two, hat beside the bed! Three, run to the pier!" The boat left, and she waved widely.

At sunset, Dad's boat returned. He lifted Riri against his chest. "Jumping up instead of counting meant you were not late at all!" Hugging his neck, she said, "Tomorrow too! Hear putt, putt, putt—jump up!"
